subtype: Approach: planning fallacy with an optimistic timetable [Pitfall]
passage: Note, Monday, by Ritu, Maths tutor. Dhruv showed me his weekend plan on Friday: ten chapters between Saturday morning and Sunday night, with no breaks written in. I asked if that was realistic. "Of course," he said. "I am fast." On Sunday evening he arrived with three chapters done and a very flat face. "I have wasted two days," he said. The plan he wrote for the next week was half-hearted: "chapters, if time". I did not scold him. I suggested we find out how long one chapter really takes him, and he agreed to time the next three. I think the problem is the estimate, not the effort.

qa.q: How many chapters did Dhruv complete over the weekend?
What was Dhruv feeling when he arrived on Sunday evening?
qa.a: Discouraged, since his face was flat and he called the weekend wasted.

qa.q: What approach could give Dhruv a better plan?
qa.a: Time how long a chapter really takes and plan from that, adding some spare time, because estimates then match reality.

qa.q: How might Ritu see Dhruv's setback?
qa.a: As a problem of estimating rather than laziness, since Ritu did not scold and suggested timing the chapters.

grounding: A student schedules ten chapters into one weekend, finishes three, and the discouragement loosens the next plan.

subtype: Approach: planning fallacy with an optimistic timetable [Pitfall]
passage:
Sunday, 10 pm
Friday night I made the Great Weekend Plan: ten History and Geography chapters, five on Saturday, five today. I even drew little clocks next to each one. I figured if I just sat down and nothing went wrong, it would work. Things went wrong. On Saturday the chapter on nationalism took four hours on its own. Kunal came over to borrow a charger and stayed for an hour. Masi dropped in for lunch. Today I did the maps chapter and stopped. Three. Three chapters out of ten. I feel like a joke. For next week I've written "finish History" on a sticky note, no dates, nothing. Honestly, I don't know if I'll even look at it.
Hansa

qa.q: How many chapters did Hansa finish over the weekend?
How does Hansa feel on Sunday night?
qa.a: Hansa feels discouraged and ashamed, calling the result a joke after hoping the weekend would go smoothly.

qa.q: What would you change first in Hansa's next plan?
qa.a: Plan two or three chapters for a weekend and leave spare time for visitors and long chapters, so the plan can actually be finished and confidence can return.

qa.q: How might Kunal see the hour-long visit?
qa.a: Kunal probably thought it was a harmless chat, with no idea it knocked a hole in a plan that had no room for anything.

grounding: A diary shows a student cramming ten chapters into one weekend, finishing three, and loosening the next plan out of discouragement.
